reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / relevant specialty textbook
clinicalPearls: Caused by a postzygotic activating (gain-of-function) variant in GNAS, producing somatic mosaicism, so the condition is not inherited and severity depends on the distribution of affected tissues
Classic triad comprises fibrous dysplasia of bone, cafe-au-lait skin macules and one or more hyperfunctioning endocrinopathies
Cafe-au-lait patches characteristically have irregular jagged (coast-of-Maine) borders and often respect the midline
Gonadotropin-independent precocious puberty is a common early presentation, frequently as the first sign in girls
Other endocrine features include hyperthyroidism, growth hormone excess, Cushing syndrome and phosphaturic renal phosphate wasting
Fibrous dysplasia can be monostotic or polyostotic, causing bone pain, deformity, fracture and, in the skull base, nerve compression
The GNAS variant constitutively activates the alpha subunit of the stimulatory G protein, driving cyclic-AMP overproduction and autonomous hormone secretion and cell proliferation
reference.pathophysiology: McCune-Albright syndrome results from an activating variant in GNAS occurring after fertilisation, producing a mosaic distribution of affected cells; a germline variant would be lethal, which explains why the condition arises only as somatic mosaicism. The variant renders the alpha subunit of the stimulatory G protein constitutively active, leading to unregulated adenylate cyclase activity and elevated intracellular cyclic AMP. In hormone-responsive endocrine tissues this drives autonomous hormone secretion independent of normal control, while in bone-forming cells it produces the fibrous dysplasia lesions. The pattern and severity of disease reflect which tissues carry the variant and in what proportion.
additionalDifferentials: Neurofibromatosis type 1 with cafe-au-lait macules (smooth coast-of-California borders)
Central (gonadotropin-dependent) precocious puberty from other causes
Isolated fibrous dysplasia without endocrine features
Other causes of hyperthyroidism, Cushing syndrome or acromegaly
Other mosaic overgrowth or RASopathy syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Molecular testing for the GNAS activating variant, ideally on affected tissue given mosaicism
Skeletal survey or radionuclide bone scan to map fibrous dysplasia
Endocrine biochemistry for precocious puberty, thyroid function, growth hormone/IGF-1 and cortisol
Serum phosphate and markers of renal phosphate wasting (including FGF23-related studies)
Cross-sectional imaging of skull base for optic or auditory canal involvement
Bone-specific imaging and biopsy where malignant transformation is suspected
redFlags: Rapidly progressive skull-base fibrous dysplasia threatening the optic nerve or hearing
Pathological fracture or severe progressive bone deformity
Rapid onset of precocious puberty or signs of severe endocrine excess
New pain, swelling or radiographic change suggesting rare malignant transformation of fibrous dysplasia
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is highly variable and depends on the extent and location of affected tissues, ranging from mild monostotic disease to severe polyostotic bone disease with multiple endocrinopathies. Malignant transformation of fibrous dysplasia is rare, and most morbidity relates to skeletal complications and hormonal excess, which are managed rather than cured.
pitfalls: Testing blood alone and missing a low-level mosaic GNAS variant that is detectable in affected tissue
Confusing the coast-of-Maine cafe-au-lait borders with the smoother lesions of neurofibromatosis type 1
Overlooking phosphate wasting as a treatable contributor to bone disease
Assuming precocious puberty is centrally driven and giving inappropriate GnRH-analogue therapy
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Treat gonadotropin-independent precocious puberty with aromatase inhibitors (letrozole) or tamoxifen, as GnRH analogues are ineffective in the peripheral form
Manage autonomous hyperthyroidism with thionamides, progressing to thyroidectomy, and treat growth hormone excess with somatostatin analogues or pegvisomant
Bisphosphonates for fibrous dysplasia bone pain, with orthopaedic fixation and deformity correction
Replace phosphate and give active vitamin D for FGF23-mediated renal phosphate wasting
Surveillance for skull-base fibrous dysplasia causing optic or auditory canal compression, and rare malignant transformation
Explain that the postzygotic GNAS mosaicism is sporadic with negligible recurrence and transmission risk, so routine family screening is not required
Coordinated multidisciplinary follow-up across endocrinology, orthopaedics and clinical genetics
